item.title: AI stocks: Midterm elections could threaten AI trade as data center backlash grows
item.description: Public opposition to US data centers and the November midterm elections could reshape AI infrastructure investment. Increased regulatory scrutiny, rising electricity costs and construction delays may pressure technology stocks, utilities and power infrastructure companies, despite continued strong AI spending.
item.dc:creator: Anupam Nagar
item.content:encoded: Public opposition to data centers is emerging as a potential risk to the artificial intelligence investment boom. The outcome of the November 3 US midterm elections is likely to influence the regulatory environment surrounding the industry's rapid expansion, Reuters reported.Artificial intelligence has been a key driver of the US stock market's four-year bull run, as major technology companies, including Alphabet and Amazon, continue to commit billions of dollars to developing data centers and other AI infrastructure. Spending on AI infrastructure is expected to exceed $1 trillion next year, supporting corporate earnings and investor optimism about the technology's growth prospects, Reuters reported.Also Read: Michael Burry bets against these 4 AI stocks, one of which rallied 190% YTDHowever, growing resistance to data center construction is raising concerns about whether the pace of investment can be sustained. Communities across the United States are increasingly worried about the environmental impact of large facilities, rising electricity costs and the broader implications of AI adoption.The issue has become increasingly relevant for financial markets, where investors have closely monitored capital expenditure plans by major technology companies as an indicator of the AI boom's strength. Recent concerns about debt levels in the cloud computing sector, particularly around CoreWeave, have already unsettled parts of the AI trade, highlighting the market's sensitivity to potential obstacles to expansion, Reuters reported.Also Read: South Korean shares fall 2% as AI selloff weighs on global marketsDemocratic victory could increase regulatory scrutinyA Democratic victory in both chambers of Congress would represent a significant political shift, transferring control of the House of Representatives and Senate from President Donald Trump's Republican Party. Such an outcome could increase scrutiny of AI companies and data center development, even if sweeping legislation to restrict construction remains unlikely.Trading on prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket has indicated that a Democratic sweep is the most likely outcome. Investors are therefore assessing how a change in congressional leadership could affect the industry's regulatory outlook, Reuters reported.According to Reuters, analysts expect Democratic control of Congress to result in more hearings and investigations into AI development, data center construction and their broader economic and environmental consequences. Although such scrutiny may not directly halt investment, it could generate negative headlines and increase uncertainty for companies planning large infrastructure projects.Read more: Japan’s Nikkei falls over 1% as Wall Street tech selloff rattles marketsPublic opposition to data centers is not confined to Democratic voters. However, a Reuters/Ipsos poll released this month found that 69% of registered Democratic voters supported limits on data center construction, compared with 43% of Republican voters.Despite the possibility of increased oversight, analysts remain sceptical that Congress would pass legislation capable of significantly slowing the industry's expansion. Trump has supported AI development and would likely oppose measures that substantially constrain investment, analysts said.Trump also said on Wednesday that companies building data centers should provide a dividend to local communities to improve public acceptance of such projects.Economic growth and competition with China could provide additional reasons for lawmakers from both parties to avoid measures that significantly impede the industry's development.Nevertheless, greater congressional scrutiny could increase volatility in AI-related stocks as investors respond to investigations, regulatory proposals and uncertainty over future investment plans, Reuters reported.State and local elections could have a direct impactBeyond the congressional contest, investors are closely monitoring state and local elections, where authorities have considerable influence over data center development, electricity infrastructure and permitting decisions.Several states, including Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Nevada, Wisconsin and Michigan, are drawing attention from investment strategists tracking gubernatorial and legislative races. Individual elections involving utility regulators could also influence the cost and pace of new projects.According to Reuters, state and local governments can play a major role in shaping the restrictions and regulatory requirements data center operators face. Election outcomes could therefore directly affect companies seeking to expand their infrastructure footprint.The geographic concentration of data center investment makes these contests particularly important for investors. Changes in local leadership or regulatory priorities could affect construction schedules, electricity expenses and the financial viability of proposed facilities.AI investment outlook remains intact, but costs could riseMarket strategists broadly expect the AI investment theme to remain intact, given the technology's strategic importance and the scale of spending planned by major technology companies. However, political opposition could complicate the industry's expansion by increasing regulatory uncertainty, delaying projects and raising operating costs.Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth, said policy uncertainty was unlikely to derail the broader AI investment theme but could disrupt the timing and cost of infrastructure development, Reuters reported.For investors, the midterm elections introduce another variable into a market increasingly dependent on sustained AI spending. While a Democratic victory may not halt data center construction outright, greater oversight and tougher local regulations could challenge assumptions about the speed and profitability of the next phase of the AI boom.The outcome could therefore influence not only technology stocks but also utilities, power infrastructure providers and other companies benefiting from the expansion of data centers across the United States.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

item.title: Nasdaq CEO flags IPO slowdown amid market volatility
item.description: The IPO market is grappling with hurdles stemming from macroeconomic instability and fluctuating market conditions that are influencing corporate strategies. Numerous firms have either delayed or abandoned their public listing intentions lately. Nevertheless, Nasdaq maintains a sturdy and vibrant pipeline for future listings, even as analysts caution that a revival in IPO activity likely won't materialize until 2026 without a surge in investor interest.
item.dc:creator: Anupam Nagar
item.content:encoded: The initial public offering market has softened modestly as macroeconomic uncertainty and market volatility prompt companies to reconsider the timing of their public debuts, Reuters reported, citing comments from the Nasdaq's chief executive.Adena Friedman said during Nasdaq's third-quarter earnings call that the long-term pipeline of companies preparing to go public remained robust, although businesses in certain sectors were reassessing their listing timelines amid an uncertain economic environment.Read more: Japan’s Nikkei falls over 1% as Wall Street tech selloff rattles marketsEscalating conflict in the Middle East has fuelled an energy price shock, reviving concerns about global inflation and complicating the monetary policy outlook. Higher borrowing costs and elevated US Treasury yields have also weighed on investor risk appetite, making public offerings more challenging for prospective issuers.According to Reuters, the deteriorating market environment has contributed to a slowdown in IPO activity over the past two months, with several companies postponing or withdrawing their planned listings.Wearable health technology company Oura postponed its planned Nasdaq debut in September, citing volatilemarket conditions. Nuclear equipment maker Holtec Nuclear also withdrew its planned US IPO amid unfavourable sentiment in equity markets and the nuclear sector. Several other companies delayed their offerings during the same period.Nasdaq recorded 167 new listings in the third quarter, compared with 205 in the year-earlier period, Reuters reported. The decline highlights the challenges facing the IPO market despite continued interest from companies seeking access to public capital.Friedman said Nasdaq's listings pipeline remained strong and that the exchange was well positioned to support companies preparing to enter the public markets. However, near-term uncertainty continues to cloud the outlook for a broader recovery in IPO activity.Read more: South Korean shares fall 2% as AI selloff weighs on global marketsMatt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, an IPO-focused research and exchange-traded fund provider, said a significant rebound in listings before the end of 2026 appeared unlikely unless enthusiasm for artificial intelligence stocks returned strongly.Kennedy added that although many companies were preparing for potential public offerings, an increasing number were shifting their timelines to 2027. Anthropic and the biotechnology sector are expected to be among the key areas of focus for the US IPO market in 2026, he said.Meanwhile, Nasdaq reported quarterly earnings above analysts' estimates on Thursday. Its shares rose 6.7% in morning trading, Reuters reported, as investors responded positively to the company's financial results despite the softer outlook for IPO activity.The strength of Nasdaq's long-term listings pipeline suggests that companies continue to view public markets as an important source of capital. However, economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions and volatile investor sentiment could continue to influence the timing of new offerings in the coming months.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
